whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Heroku Architect exam for?

personas.label: Hands-on practitioners
personas.description: You build and operate Heroku applications and make choices about scale, security and availability.

personas.label: Solution designers
personas.description: You design solutions that connect Heroku apps with Salesforce and other services.

personas.label: Career builders
personas.description: You are moving into architecture work for applications that combine Salesforce and custom code.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Heroku Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: The exam covers Heroku architecture, including dynos, networking, data services, deployment and Salesforce integration. Choose an approach that meets the stated workload and operating requirements.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
72% to pass, which is 44 correct answers out of 60.
Architecture choices: Compare runtimes, data services, and scaling approaches.
Salesforce integration: Review Heroku Connect, events, and APIs.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Use practice tests to find areas to revisit. Before booking, practise explaining how your design would handle a dyno or database failure.

examFormat.heading: Heroku Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The exam can be taken online with a proctor or at a test centre. Check the current exam guide for the latest requirements.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Scenarios describe an application and its needs, such as scale, network access, data handling or availability. Match the design to those constraints.
bestWayToPass: Choose a runtime and network design that meets the stated security requirement.
Use workers and queues for long-running work; keep web requests short.
Match the database, cache and event service to the data workload.
Plan deployment, recovery and Salesforce synchronization together.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers designing Heroku applications that scale, meet security needs and work with Salesforce. Topics include runtimes, data services, deployment and integration. The exam is 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, with a 72% pass mark, weighted towards Heroku Enterprise (28%) and Data (17%).

keyConcepts.h2: Heroku Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Heroku Platform Architecture & Dynos
blocks.body: Heroku apps run in dynos. Web dynos handle HTTP requests, worker dynos run background jobs, and one-off dynos run administrative tasks. Dyno filesystems are ephemeral, so persistent files belong in a database or object store. Heroku’s router imposes a request time limit, so move long-running work to an asynchronous job. Scale an app by adding dynos or selecting a larger dyno type, as supported by the plan.

blocks.heading: Data Services: Heroku Postgres & Redis
blocks.body: Heroku Postgres supports followers for read workloads and high-availability options on eligible plans. A follower is read-only. Connection pooling can reduce the number of database connections used by app processes. Heroku Key-Value Store provides Redis-compatible storage for caching and other fast key-value needs. Check current product availability and plan limits before selecting a service.

blocks.heading: CI/CD, Review Apps & Release Management
blocks.body: A **pipeline** helps a team promote a tested build from one stage to another, such as staging to production. **Review apps** provide temporary environments for pull requests, and **Heroku CI** can run tests. Review how buildpacks or container images produce a release, how **config vars** hold environment-specific settings, and how the **release phase** runs tasks such as migrations before a release is deployed. Practise rolling back when a release fails.

blocks.heading: Security, Compliance & Private Spaces
blocks.body: The **Common Runtime** is shared; **Private Spaces** provide isolated networking in a selected region and offer options such as private connectivity. **Shield Private Spaces** add controls for workloads with stricter requirements. Review Enterprise team permissions and SSO, and restrict access to settings and secrets.

blocks.heading: Architecture Patterns for Salesforce + Heroku
blocks.body: **Heroku Connect** can synchronize Salesforce data and Heroku Postgres. For event-driven integration, compare **Platform Events** with **Change Data Capture**. For direct requests, review the Salesforce REST API, Heroku AppLink, and External Services. Choose a pattern based on data volume, consistency, access, and the system that owns the data.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Heroku Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: List the app’s workload, network, security and availability constraints before choosing a Heroku design.

blocks.heading: Use the right process type
blocks.body: Web dynos serve requests; workers handle background jobs; one-off dynos run administrative tasks.

blocks.heading: Keep durable data off dyno disk
blocks.body: Dyno filesystems are ephemeral. Store persistent files in a database or object store.

blocks.heading: Scale data services deliberately
blocks.body: Followers can serve read workloads; high availability and connection pooling address different database needs.

blocks.heading: Select network isolation to fit
blocks.body: Private Spaces provide network isolation and stable outbound IPs; evaluate Shield features against specific compliance requirements.

blocks.heading: Choose the Salesforce link
blocks.body: Heroku Connect syncs mapped Salesforce data with Postgres; events and APIs support other integration patterns.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Architect Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After Heroku Architect, many people move toward the wider Salesforce architect credentials:

sampleQuestions.question: How should the architect handle PDF generation that takes longer than a Heroku web request allows?
options: Queue PDF work on a worker
Ask users to refresh the page after each timeout
Move the long task to a larger web dyno
sampleQuestions.explanation: Queue PDF work on a worker is the best fit because the router drops requests over 30 seconds. Background work on a worker dyno avoids the limit and keeps web dynos free.
whyWrong: Ask users to refresh the page after each timeout is not the best choice because refreshing just starts the same slow request again.
Move the long task to a larger web dyno is not the best choice because a larger dyno may be faster but can still pass 30 seconds.
Disable the router’s request limit is not the best choice because you can't turn off the router timeout.

sampleQuestions.question: Why can files saved to a dyno’s local disk disappear?
options: The images exceed a size limit
sampleQuestions.explanation: Ephemeral dyno filesystem is the best fit because dynos are restarted at least daily and their disk is wiped. Files must go to a store like S3.
whyWrong: The images exceed a size limit is not the best choice because the images weren't in the database.
The database is full is not the best choice because it does not meet the scenario as directly as Dyno disk is temporary and is cleared on restart.
Heroku removes images by policy is not the best choice because heroku doesn't target images. The whole local disk is temporary.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Heroku environment should be evaluated for an app with demanding security and compliance needs?
options: Use a free dyno without a compliance review
Run the task as a one-off dyno
Assume Common Runtime meets every requirement
sampleQuestions.explanation: Shield Private Space is the best fit because shield Private Spaces add the extra isolation, logging and encryption controls needed for regulated data such as health records.
whyWrong: Use a free dyno without a compliance review is not the best choice because free or hobby dynos are not suitable for production or compliance.
Run the task as a one-off dyno is not the best choice because one-off dynos are for admin tasks, not a runtime choice.
Assume Common Runtime meets every requirement is not the best choice because the Common Runtime is shared and not built for regulated data.

sampleQuestions.question: What can move reporting queries off the primary Heroku Postgres database?
options: Create an empty database on another app
sampleQuestions.explanation: Postgres follower for reporting is the best fit because a follower is a read-only copy that stays in sync. Reports can run on it without slowing the main database.
whyWrong: Create an empty database on another app is not the best choice because a fork is a one-time copy that quickly goes out of date.
Fork the database daily is not the best choice because it does not meet the scenario as directly as Add a read-only Postgres follower for reports.
Add more web dynos is not the best choice because more web dynos don't reduce database load.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Heroku network option provides stable outbound IP addresses for a partner allowlist?
options: Private Spaces with stable outbound IPs
Call the API from the visitor’s browser
sampleQuestions.explanation: Private Spaces with stable outbound IPs is the best fit because private Spaces give the app fixed outbound IPs that the partner can allow.
whyWrong: Common Runtime with changing IPs is not the best choice because it does not meet the scenario as directly as Private Spaces with stable outbound IPs.
Call the API from the visitor’s browser is not the best choice because browser calls come from users' IPs, which are unknown.
Use a larger dyno is not the best choice because dyno size doesn't change the IP address.

sampleQuestions.question: How can a Heroku portal query Salesforce data locally without making an API request for every page view?
options: Call Salesforce for each page the customer opens
Put Salesforce rows in config vars
Load a CSV export once a week
sampleQuestions.explanation: Heroku Connect sync to Postgres is the best fit because heroku Connect keeps a copy of Salesforce data in Postgres, so the app reads it locally with fast SQL queries.
whyWrong: Call Salesforce for each page the customer opens is not the best choice because an API call per page view uses up limits and is slower.
Put Salesforce rows in config vars is not the best choice because config vars are for settings, not data.
Load a CSV export once a week is not the best choice because a weekly CSV is out of date.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Heroku feature creates a temporary test app for each pull request?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Review Apps is the best fit because review apps spin up a fresh app for each pull request and remove it when the pull request is closed.
whyWrong: Release Phase is not the best choice because promotion moves an existing build between stages. It doesn't create per-PR apps.
Pipeline promotion is not the best choice because one-off dynos run single commands.
One-off dynos is not the best choice because it does not meet the scenario as directly as Review Apps.

sampleQuestions.question: After staging sign-off, which Pipeline action moves the tested artifact into production without rebuilding it?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Promote copies the existing slug from staging to production, preserving the artifact that passed testing.
whyWrong: Push and rebuild from source is not the best choice because copying by hand is error-prone.
Copy files manually is not the best choice because a different buildpack produces a different build.
Rebuild with another buildpack is not the best choice because it does not meet the scenario as directly as Promote the existing build through the Pipeline.

sampleQuestions.question: Where should a database migration run so it completes before the new app dynos start?
options: Run them on the first web request
sampleQuestions.explanation: Release-phase migration is the best fit because release phase commands run after the build and before new dynos start, so the database is ready first.
whyWrong: Run them manually after deploy is not the best choice because running on the first request can cause errors for users.
Run them on the first web request is not the best choice because it does not meet the scenario as directly as Run migrations in the release phase.
Run them in a browser is not the best choice because browsers can't run database migrations.

sampleQuestions.question: How can a Heroku app receive near-real-time notice of a closed Salesforce Opportunity?
options: Ask a sales rep to send email
sampleQuestions.explanation: Change Data Capture is the best fit because events push the change to the app as it happens, without polling.
whyWrong: Export data weekly is not the best choice because it does not meet the scenario as directly as Subscribe to Salesforce Change Data Capture.
Poll every hour is not the best choice because hourly polling is slow and wastes API calls.
Ask a sales rep to send email is not the best choice because email isn't an integration.

sampleQuestions.question: A production app must use its own database credential, kept out of the repository. Where should the architect set that value?
options: Put it in a code comment
sampleQuestions.explanation: Store the credential as a config var for the production app. Heroku supplies it at runtime, so it stays out of source and can differ by environment.
whyWrong: Put it in a code comment is not the best choice because the secret is still in the repository, just harder to read.
Encrypt the source file is not the best choice because it does not meet the scenario as directly as Store the password in a config var.
Add it to the README is not the best choice because a README is even more visible.

sampleQuestions.question: What can reduce database connection pressure when many dynos connect to Postgres?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Use connection pooling is the best fit because connection pooling shares a smaller number of database connections between many app processes.
whyWrong: Add web dynos is not the best choice because more dynos would open even more connections.
Remove database indexes is not the best choice because removing indexes slows queries and doesn't reduce connections.
Restart Postgres hourly is not the best choice because restarts cause downtime and don't fix the cause.

sampleQuestions.question: What database capability helps the production database recover if its primary server fails?
options: Use a reporting follower as primary
sampleQuestions.explanation: High-availability Postgres plan is the best fit because high-availability plans keep a standby that takes over automatically if the primary fails.
whyWrong: Use daily backups alone is not the best choice because it does not meet the scenario as directly as Choose an eligible Heroku Postgres high-availability plan.
Use a reporting follower as primary is not the best choice because a follower can be promoted by hand, but it isn't an automatic failover plan.
Add a larger dyno is not the best choice because dyno size doesn't protect the database.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Heroku data service can provide a fast cache for sessions and frequently read values?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Key-Value Store is the best fit because key-Value Store (Redis-compatible) is built for fast caching and session storage.
whyWrong: A Postgres follower is not the best choice because config vars are for settings.
Config vars is not the best choice because local disk is wiped on restart and isn't shared between dynos.
Dyno local disk is not the best choice because it does not meet the scenario as directly as Heroku Key-Value Store.

sampleQuestions.question: Which managed service fits high-volume event streams consumed by multiple services?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Apache Kafka on Heroku is the best fit because kafka is built for high-volume event streams, and new consumers can read the same stream without changing producers.
whyWrong: Log files is not the best choice because it does not meet the scenario as directly as Apache Kafka on Heroku.
Polling a table is not the best choice because polling a table doesn't scale to high volume.
Direct calls between every service is not the best choice because point-to-point calls tie services together and grow messy.
